name: Payot

lead: Payot (pe'ot, meaning 'corners') are the sidelocks of hair left uncut at the temples by many Orthodox Jewish men, following a Torah commandment about not rounding the corners of the head.

In style terms they frame the face and signal community identity, with styles ranging from short sideburns to long curls. They are documented here as a grooming and style tradition, not a looks treatment.

paras: Hair in the temple area is left uncut, then grown out, curled, twisted, tucked behind the ears or brushed straight, depending on the community. Styles are taught within families and communities.
No health risks are associated. As a religious practice, it has been subject to bans, such as one in the Russian Empire in 1845.

angle.text: Payot are a grooming choice that changes the outline of the hairstyle around the face. Style varies from tucked to long curls, and the look signals community.

lead: Payot, also spelled peyot or pe'ot ('corners' in Hebrew), are sidelocks worn by some Orthodox Jewish men. They derive from Leviticus 19:27, which forbids rounding off the corner of the head [1][2].

The Talmud (Makkot 20a) understood the corner to mean the hair in front of the ears, down to beneath the cheekbone, and the Mishnah applied the rule only to men [1]. Communities interpret the minimum differently, from short sideburns to long locks.
As a grooming style, payot frame the face and mark the wearer's community. Hasidic and Yemenite Jews often grow them long; some Haredi men trim them or tuck them behind the ears [1].

paras: The halakhic literature debates the exact location of the payot and what removing them prohibits [1]. Maimonides regarded shaving the sidelocks as a heathen practice [1]. Boys typically receive a first haircut at age three at the upsherinish, after which the sidelocks are kept [2].

Yemenite Jews wear long, thin twisted locks called simanim, sometimes reaching the upper arm. Satmar men wear thick sidelocks tucked behind the ears, Belz men wrap them around the ears, Skver men wear tight coils in front of the ear, and the Brisk movement brushes hair straight down [1].

The custom of long payot spread into Slavic lands alongside Kabbalistic teachings, and in 1845 the practice was banned in the Russian Empire [1]. Crimean Tatars used the term 'Jews with payot' for the Krymchaks [1].
